metadata.title: PISA 2022 Results (Volume II): Learning During – and From – Disruption

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This volume reports PISA 2022 results for the target population of 15-year-old students, using PISA’s international sampling and scaling procedures. The report notes that where principals’ questionnaire responses are presented, they are weighted to be proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school, indicating the use of complex survey weighting at least for school-level questionnaire summaries. For student-level results, the publication discusses sampling standards (exclusion rates, school response rates, student response rates) and the need for caution when standards are not met, which is consistent with weighted estimation under a complex design. The document excerpt provided does not specify the exact student weight variable name(s) or replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so the precise weighting implementation cannot be fully reconstructed from the text shown.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is an OECD PISA results volume that synthesises descriptive and comparative findings rather than estimating a student-level predictive model with explicitly documented plausible-value (PV) and missing-data procedures in the provided text. PISA cognitive achievement is typically reported on the PISA scale using scaling and comparability procedures, but the excerpt does not describe a PV-based analytic pipeline (e.g., Rubin’s rules) or a specific missing-data handling method for an ML model. Therefore, missing-data handling is treated as not reported for the purposes of this extraction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report states that PISA 2022 collected data from nearly 700 000 students aged 15 years (15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months) enrolled in school and having completed at least 6 years of formal schooling, across 81 OECD Member and partner economies. The excerpt does not provide a chapter-specific analytic subsample definition (e.g., which domains/indicators were restricted to particular student groups), but it does describe that some entities were adjudicated with annotations due to not meeting sampling standards (overall exclusion rate, school response rate, student response rate) and that caution is required for those estimates. For the purposes of this extraction, the analytic sample is treated as the full available PISA 2022 target population for the participating entities, with results annotated where sampling standards were not met.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2022 Results (Volume II) synthesises cross-country evidence on how education systems maintained learning during COVID-19 disruptions and how they supported student well-being and equity. The volume reports that nearly 700 000 students from 81 OECD Member and partner economies participated, and it compares performance and related indicators to PISA 2018 to assess changes over time. It explains that PISA scores are scaled to the PISA metric and interpreted via proficiency levels, and it highlights that statistical significance is assessed at the 5% level with attention to sampling and measurement uncertainty. The report also documents limitations for 13 adjudicated entities where sampling standards (exclusion, school response, student response) were not met, which can affect the comparability of estimates. In the provided excerpt, no student-level predictive modelling or ML pipeline is described; instead, the volume uses PISA’s established assessment and reporting framework to produce descriptive and comparative policy-relevant insights.
